data.title: The Zbruch Idol – a four-sided image of a Slavic god
data.excerpt: A four-sided stone pillar 2.67 m high, raised from the bed of the river Zbruch in 1848, is a well-known image of a pagan Slavic deity. Each of its sides is divided into three bands – the world of the gods, of people and of the underworld – and bears one of four figures, which may be four separate gods, or a single four-headed Svantovít.

children.text: A well-known statue discovered by archaeologists in 1848, but not attested in written sources, is the so-called Zbruch Idol. Three pairs of oxen were needed to raise the large stone block from the bed of the river. The idol probably comes from the site of Bogit by the Zbruch (on the boundary of the Ternopil and Khmelnytskyi oblasts), 1.5 km from the place where it was found, where a small circular sanctuary was discovered consisting of eight bowl-shaped hollows and one central post, which was set in a pit lined with stones.

children.text: The Zbruch Idol is a four-sided stone pillar 2.67 m high, with sides 29–32 cm wide, weighing approximately half a tonne. Each side of the pillar is divided into three bands. The decoration of the three bands, which are placed one above the other, is interpreted as depicting, from the top, the world of the gods, which holds the highest power and is therefore the largest; below it the world of people, who are tiny in comparison with the gods; and lowest of all the world of the underworld, which supports the spheres above it and whose representatives are shown in considerably contorted forms. The top is distinctly worked on all four sides into the shape of a human figure with a hat and without a moustache. Two of the large figures are interpreted as male and two as female. Each of them is rendered a little differently and holds different attributes. The first woman holds a drinking horn (or a horn of plenty?) in her right hand; she could probably represent a goddess of fertility. The man on the second edge is shown with a curved sword (a sabre?) typical of the 9th–11th century. On the third side there is the figure of a man whose hands are empty, but lower down on the pillar there is a circular symbol, which is interpreted as a symbol of the sun, and the figure is therefore identified as a sun god. On the last side a woman with a ring in her hand is depicted. There are no analogies to this unique find, although primitive many-headed figurines are known from Poland, Bulgaria, Ukraine and Novgorod. Because the chronicler Saxo Grammaticus’s description of Svantovít at Arkona is known, and because it agrees with the Zbruch Idol in several attributes, some specialists claim that the Zbruch Idol depicts only a single god, precisely the four-headed Svantovít. It is, however, far more likely that each side of the idol depicts a different figure, a different god. The Bogit hillfort belongs among the so-called sacred hillforts, which had a sacral area, ramparts, ditches and several buildings, but it was evidently never inhabited. Farm buildings were absent as well. Even the ramparts themselves were symbolic rather than of any functional value. In the vicinity of this sacral place the remains of a building were found which, given the valuable finds, was interpreted as a probable treasury. In their article Vo vremena zbručskogo idola, the authors Rusanova and Timoshchuk put forward the theory that the statue found here was venerated until the middle of the 13th century.

children.text: The Zbruch Idol is exceptional also in being four-sided; round pits for statues representing a god are found far more often. Given the workmanship and the polycephaly of the statue, which also bears certain attributes of a deity, its cult character is very likely. A question raised by some researchers is whether its makers really were the ancient Slavs. The fact that it is a stone and not a wooden statue, as is typical for the Slavs, and that the attribute of one of the figures is a curved sabre instead of the typical sword or axe, leads to the supposition that it could be the work of steppe nomads. The Turko-Tatars created stone “babas” – anthropomorphic images that were supposed to depict dead warriors. This is shown by their custom of depicting figures on a stone stele (unlike the Slavs), but even for this culture the Zbruch Idol would be entirely unique.
The article is taken from the diploma thesis of Barbora Bílková, Kultovní lokality slovanského archaického náboženství (Locations of Cult of Slavic Archaic Religion), University of Pardubice, 2014.
